Directly in front of him, in the pale moonlight, stood a terrifying old man. His eyes glowed like red-hot coals. Long gray hair hung in tangled ropes over his shoulders. His clothes were old-fashioned, filthy, and torn, and heavy, rusty chains and shackles hung from his wrists and ankles.

“My dear sir,” said Mr. Otis, “I really must ask you to oil those chains. I've brought a small bottle of Tammany Rising Sun Lubricator for that very purpose. They say a single application solves the problem completely. You'll find statements confirming this on the wrapper from several of our most distinguished American clergymen. I'll leave it here beside the bedroom candles and will gladly provide more if you need it.” With that, the United States Minister put the bottle on a marble table, shut his door, and returned to bed.

For a moment the Canterville ghost stood perfectly still, understandably outraged. Then he hurled the bottle onto the polished floor and fled along the corridor, groaning hollowly and giving off an eerie green light. But just as he reached the top of the great oak staircase, a door flew open. Two small figures in white nightclothes appeared, and a large pillow whistled past his head. There was clearly no time to lose. He quickly escaped by using the Fourth Dimension of Space, vanished through the wooden wall panels, and left the house completely quiet.

When he reached a small hidden room in the left wing, he leaned against a moonbeam to catch his breath and tried to understand what had happened. In a brilliant career lasting three hundred uninterrupted years, he had never suffered such a terrible insult. He remembered the widowed Duchess, whom he had frightened into a fit as she stood at her mirror in lace and diamonds. He thought of the four housemaids who had become hysterical when he simply grinned at them through the curtains of a spare bedroom. There was the parish rector, whose candle he had blown out one night as the man left the library late. Ever since, the rector had suffered terribly from nervous troubles and remained under Sir William Gull's care. Then there was old Madame de Tremouillac. Waking early one morning, she had seen a skeleton in an armchair beside the fire, reading her diary. The resulting brain fever had kept her in bed for six weeks. After she recovered, she had returned to the Church and ended her friendship with that notorious religious skeptic, Monsieur de Voltaire.

“Oh, I misunderstood. I thought you said ‘anybody,’ so I assumed that meant—well, anybody. Everyone, in fact.”

“It does mean anybody—anybody of noble birth. And royalty is better still.”

“That seems quite reasonable,” said the abbot, seeing a chance to calm things down and prevent trouble. “Such a wonderful gift would hardly be given to reveal the affairs of people below those born close to the heights of greatness. Our King Arthur—”

“Would you like news of him?” the enchanter interrupted.

“Very gladly, yes, and with gratitude.”

At once everyone was full of wonder and interest again, the hopeless fools. They watched his spells with complete attention. When he made his announcement, they looked at me as if to say, “There, what do you think of that?”

“The king is tired from hunting. For the past two hours he has lain in his palace, sleeping without dreams.”

“God bless him!” said the abbot, crossing himself. “May that sleep refresh both his body and his soul.”

“It might, if he were asleep,” I said. “But the king isn't sleeping. He's riding.”

That brought trouble again: two authorities saying opposite things. Nobody knew which of us to believe, since I still had some reputation left. The magician grew scornful.

“I have seen many remarkable fortune-tellers, prophets, and magicians in my lifetime,” he said, “but never one who could sit doing nothing and see the truth of things without a single spell to help.”

“You've been living in the woods and missed a great deal. I use spells myself, as these good brothers know—but only on important occasions.”

When it comes to sarcasm, I reckon I can hold my own. That little jab made him squirm. The abbot asked after the queen and the court, and received this answer:

“They are all asleep, worn out by tiredness, just like the king.”

I said:

“That's simply another lie. Half are enjoying their entertainments. The queen and the other half aren't asleep; they're riding. Perhaps you could make a little more effort and tell us where the king, the queen, and everyone riding with them at this moment are going?”

“They are sleeping now, as I said. Tomorrow they will ride, for they are traveling towards the sea.”

“And where will they be at evening prayers the day after tomorrow?”

“Far north of Camelot, with half their journey behind them.”

“That's another lie, wrong by a hundred and fifty miles.

Tom joined the newly formed Cadets of Temperance because their elaborate ceremonial outfits appealed to him. He pledged to give up smoking, chewing tobacco, and swearing for as long as he belonged. Then he learned something new: promising not to do a thing is the surest possible way to make yourself want to do it. Soon Tom was tortured by a longing to drink and swear. It became so powerful that only the prospect of showing off his red sash kept him from quitting. The Fourth of July was approaching, but before he had endured his restraints for even forty-eight hours, he abandoned the idea of waiting for it. Instead he pinned his hopes on old Judge Frazer, the justice of the peace, who appeared to be dying. Such an important official would certainly have a large public funeral. For three days Tom followed the Judge's condition with deep concern, eagerly seeking news. Sometimes his hopes rose enough for him to take out his outfit and practice in front of the mirror. But the Judge's condition kept changing in a most discouraging way. Finally they declared him improving, and then recovering. Tom was disgusted and felt personally wronged. He resigned immediately. That very night, the Judge relapsed and died. Tom decided he would never again trust a man like that.

The funeral was splendid. The Cadets marched in a display that nearly killed their former member with envy. Still, Tom was free again, and that counted for something. He could drink and swear now, but to his surprise he no longer wanted to. Simply being allowed to do it had removed both the desire and the attraction.

Before long Tom discovered, to his astonishment, that the vacation he had so eagerly wanted was becoming rather tedious.

He tried keeping a diary, but after three days in which nothing happened, he gave it up.

The first minstrel show portraying Black people arrived in town and caused a sensation. Tom and Joe Harper organized their own troupe of performers and enjoyed themselves for two days.

Even the glorious Fourth was something of a disappointment. Heavy rain meant there was no parade, and Mr. Benton, a real United States senator whom Tom believed to be the greatest man in the world, proved crushingly disappointing. He wasn't twenty-five feet tall, or even remotely close to it.

A circus arrived.
